name: QA engineer
summary: QA and test engineer interviews usually test how you think about what could go wrong: writing test cases for an everyday feature, reporting a bug clearly and deciding what to test first. Candidates commonly report questions on testing types and the bug life cycle, and for automation and SDET roles, coding in a language such as Java or Python plus tools like Selenium, Playwright or API testing frameworks.
rounds: Online test or written exercise: test cases for a feature, testing concepts, sometimes basic coding
Technical round on testing types, test design and the bug life cycle
Automation round for automation and SDET roles: write a test or discuss a framework
looks_for: Thinking beyond the happy path: edge cases, errors and odd inputs
Clear bug reports a developer can act on straight away
Prioritising tests by risk when time is short
Automation that is reliable and maintainable, not just recorded
Checking APIs and data, not only the user interface
Working with developers as partners on quality

questions.text: Tell me about the most important bug you've found. How did you find it?
covers: What made you look there
How you reproduced it and narrowed down the conditions
Its impact, and what happened after you reported it

questions.text: Describe a time a developer said a bug you reported wasn't a bug.
covers: The disagreement, and what the requirement actually said
How you showed the evidence calmly
How it was settled, and what you'd clarify earlier next time

questions.text: Tell me about a release where testing time was cut. What did you test, and what did you leave out?
covers: How you ranked areas by risk and by how much they're used
What you told the team about what wasn't tested
What happened after the release

questions.text: Tell me about a bug that reached production despite your testing. What did you learn?
covers: Why the tests missed it, honestly
How it was found and fixed
The change you made to your tests or process

questions.text: How would you test a login page? Talk me through the cases you'd cover.
covers: Valid and invalid logins, empty fields, case sensitivity, very long inputs
Security: locking after repeated failures, a hidden password field, injection attempts
Usability, accessibility, and different browsers and devices

questions.text: Explain verification versus validation, and functional versus non-functional testing.
covers: Verification: was it built right? Validation: was the right thing built?
Functional tests check what it does; non-functional tests check speed, security and usability
An example of each from a project

questions.text: What's the difference between severity and priority? Give an example where they differ.
covers: Severity is the impact; priority is how soon it should be fixed
A high-severity, low-priority bug, and the reverse
Who usually decides each

questions.text: Walk me through the life of a bug, from when you find it to when it's closed.
covers: A report with steps, expected and actual results, evidence and environment
Statuses such as new, assigned, fixed, retest, closed or reopened
Retesting the fix and running regression tests around it

questions.text: What's the difference between smoke, sanity and regression testing?
covers: Smoke: is the build stable enough to test at all?
Sanity: a focused check after a small fix or change
Regression: making sure existing features still work, and why it suits automation

questions.text: How would you decide which tests to automate and which to keep manual?
covers: Automating stable, repetitive, high-value checks such as regression
Keeping exploratory, one-off and fast-changing areas manual
Weighing the cost of maintaining a test against the time it saves

questions.text: Your automated UI tests pass sometimes and fail other times with no code change. What would you do?
covers: Finding the pattern: timing, test data, test order, environment
Fixes: proper waits instead of fixed sleeps, independent test data, stable locators
Separating flaky tests so they don't hide genuine failures

questions.text: How would you structure a test automation framework so it stays easy to maintain?
covers: Page objects or similar layers that keep locators in one place
Test data and configuration kept out of the test code
Running in CI with clear reports and screenshots on failure

questions.text: How would you test a REST API, for example one that creates an order?
covers: Status codes, the response body, and the order saved correctly
Invalid input, missing fields, authentication and permissions
Tools such as Postman or code-based tests, and checking the database where needed

questions.text: Explain equivalence partitioning and boundary value analysis, using an age field that accepts 18 to 60.
covers: Grouping inputs that should behave the same and testing one from each group
Testing just below, at and just above each boundary: 17, 18, 60 and 61
Why this finds bugs with fewer test cases

questions.text: How would you approach performance testing for a ticket-booking site before a big sale?
covers: Expected load, the shape of the peak, and the key user journeys
Load and stress tests with a tool such as JMeter or k6, watching response times and errors
Finding the bottleneck with developers and testing again after fixes

questions.text: Why do you want a career in testing rather than development?
covers: What you enjoy about finding problems and protecting users
An example that shows that mindset
Where you want to grow: automation, performance, security testing

questions.text: How do you keep learning new testing tools, and what are you learning right now?
covers: A specific tool or skill you're learning, and why
How you practise it: a side project, a course, tasks at work
How it would help in this role

tips: When asked to test anything, first ask what it's for and who uses it, then list cases in groups: functional, edge, negative and non-functional.
Bring a sample bug report you've written (with nothing confidential in it) and be ready to explain why it's clear.
For automation roles, expect to write code live; practise basic programming in your test language, not only tool commands.
Be honest about which tools you've used and which you've only read about; follow-up questions find the difference quickly.
Mention API and database checks; testing only through the screen is a common gap.
